For pumps, we look at the peak demand of the baseline load shape and assume that that corresponds to the pump running at maximum capacity. An example of this model is shown in Figure 5. Here, the baseline load runs for 8 hours in the middle of the day, such that some demand occurs during hours when the price is higher than other hours of the day. The “New Load A” line represents how the load could be optimized subject to the maximum demand level observed during that day; here, the load runs for two hours in the early morning hours, then another six hours in the late morning/early afternoon. “New Load B” shows an even lower-price alternative, if the load is able to run at a higher power level than observed. Here the load (e.g., the pump) is able to meet all of the required demand in a shorter time period, running only in the four lowest-price hours of the day. Figure 5. Illustrative figure of load dispatch for an end use that is completely flexible subject to total and maximum demand constraints Several limitations of this load shifting model should be noted. Firstly, the end use is assumed to be available to run at all hours of the day. This is unlikely to be the case for EVs, which at a minimum cannot charge while they are being driven, and likely will experience significant other amounts of time when charging access is not available. For pool, spa, and irrigation pumps, operational hours may be limited by customer preferences related to noise, use of the pool/spa 15 equipment, farm labor hours, and so on. Additionally, the load is assumed to be fully flexible over a series of sequential windows, not a rolling window. For example, in one week of the year, the model may choose to do all crop irrigation on the first day, while the following week, it may choose to do all irrigation on the seventh day, leaving the crops unwatered for the entirety of the 12 days in between. This would still technically meet the “weekly” watering needs of the crops per calendar week, but in reality may not be acceptable to the service level required. 2.3.3 Battery energy storage systems (BESS) The Distributed Optimal and Predictive Energy Resources (DOPER) model is used to model the response of behind the meter storage to dynamic prices.13 DOPER is a model predictive control tool in which an internal mathematical model is evaluated and solved to a global optimum at each controller evaluation. DOPER’s capabilities are robust; but in this study we focus on using the battery charging optimization to maximize revenue in response to an hourly price signal.
